steps.action: Perform time-out: verify patient identity, procedure, levels, laterality, allergies, and anticoagulation status.
steps.safety: Confirm patient had at least 80% relief from dual comparative medial branch blocks before proceeding to RFA.
steps.teaching: RFA is indicated only after positive dual comparative diagnostic medial branch blocks. Proceeding without adequate diagnostic confirmation leads to poor outcomes and unnecessary procedures.

steps.action: Review prior MBB procedure notes to confirm exact levels and response. Plan corresponding RFA levels.
steps.safety: RFA levels must match the diagnostic MBB levels exactly. Do not add or subtract levels without additional diagnostic blocks.
steps.teaching: The RFA target is the same anatomical location as the MBB: the junction of the SAP and TP for L1-L4, and the sacral ala-S1 SAP junction for L5.

steps.action: Position patient prone. Select appropriate RF cannulae: typically 18- or 20-gauge, 10 cm length with 10 mm active tip.
steps.safety: Larger active tips create larger lesions. Match the active tip length to the anatomy (10 mm for standard lumbar RFA).
steps.teaching: The RF lesion extends laterally from the active tip, not beyond it. Proper needle placement parallel to the nerve maximizes the lesion length along the nerve course.

steps.action: Set up C-arm in AP view with squared endplates. Identify target levels and plan needle trajectories.
steps.safety: RFA cannulae are larger than MBB needles. Use local anesthesia (lidocaine) at each skin entry point.
steps.teaching: The RF cannula should be placed parallel to the medial branch nerve as it courses along the TP-SAP junction. This requires a slightly caudal-to-cephalad trajectory in most cases.

steps.action: Advance RF cannula to the TP-SAP junction (L1-L4) or sacral ala (L5) using the same fluoroscopic technique as MBB.
steps.safety: Ensure bony contact before testing. The cannula should rest on the periosteum at the nerve target.
steps.teaching: The goal is to place the active tip parallel to the medial branch nerve along the groove of the TP-SAP junction. A slightly oblique trajectory (ipsilateral oblique view) can help achieve parallel placement.

steps.action: Perform sensory stimulation at 50 Hz, up to 0.5 V. The patient should report concordant pain or pressure at or below threshold.
steps.safety: If stimulation reproduces pain at less than 0.5 V, the cannula is near the target nerve. If no response at 0.5 V, reposition.
steps.teaching: Sensory stimulation confirms proximity to the medial branch nerve. The patient should feel a deep, aching, or pressure sensation in the usual area of pain, confirming the correct nerve.

steps.action: Perform motor stimulation at 2 Hz, up to 1.0 V. Observe for multifidus fasciculation (acceptable) and rule out lower extremity motor response.
steps.safety: If lower extremity motor response occurs at less than 2x the sensory threshold, the cannula may be near a ventral ramus. Reposition to avoid motor nerve injury.
steps.teaching: Motor stimulation at 2 Hz should produce local multifidus twitching (visible or palpable paraspinal muscle contraction) but NOT limb movement. Limb movement indicates proximity to the ventral ramus or nerve root.

steps.action: Anesthetize the target with 0.5-1 mL of 2% lidocaine through the cannula prior to lesioning.
steps.safety: Local anesthesia reduces procedural pain during the thermal lesion but may temporarily affect subsequent sensory testing at adjacent levels.
steps.teaching: Pre-lesion local anesthesia is standard practice. Some practitioners complete all sensory and motor testing at all levels before anesthetizing any level to avoid cross-contamination.

steps.action: Perform conventional thermal RF lesion at 80 degrees C for 90 seconds at each level. Monitor patient throughout.
steps.safety: The patient should not experience severe radiating limb pain during lesioning. If this occurs, abort and reposition.
steps.teaching: Standard thermal RF creates an oblate spheroid lesion extending laterally from the active tip. At 80 degrees C for 90 seconds with a 10 mm active tip, the lesion is approximately 5-6 mm in diameter.

steps.action: Consider creating a second lesion at each level by slightly repositioning the cannula (bipedicular technique or rotating the cannula) to increase lesion coverage.
steps.safety: Multiple lesions per level improve success rates but increase tissue disruption. Limit to 2-3 lesions per target.
steps.teaching: Studies show that multi-lesion techniques improve denervation success rates from approximately 60% to 80%. The parallel placement technique and slight repositioning help capture anatomic variation in nerve position.

steps.action: Remove cannulae and apply bandages. Monitor patient for 20-30 minutes. Prescribe post-procedure analgesics for neuritis pain.
steps.safety: Warn patient about expected post-procedure soreness lasting 1-3 weeks (post-denervation neuritis). New radicular symptoms are NOT expected.
steps.teaching: Post-RFA neuritis (localized back soreness and stiffness) is common and expected. It typically resolves within 2-3 weeks. Therapeutic benefit from RFA may take 3-6 weeks to fully manifest.

steps.action: Schedule follow-up at 4-6 weeks. Document all levels treated, RF parameters, stimulation thresholds, and number of lesions per level.
steps.safety: Assess pain relief at follow-up. Successful RFA typically provides 6-12 months of relief before nerve regeneration.
steps.teaching: Medial branch nerves regenerate over 6-18 months. When pain returns to pre-RFA levels, repeat diagnostic blocks may be performed, and RFA can be repeated with similar success rates.
